text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--Danish inland revenue chiefs call for more autonomy and less control from the Ministry of Taxation in collecting taxes and duties. They claim that tax collection would be more effective and swifter if the ministry had less of a say in inland revenue budgetting and staffing. The Danish inland revenue has a staff of 6,000 nationwide.

--Stormy weather and rough seas at the weekend delayed the sinking of a 20,000 tonne caisson into the seabed off the coast near Copenhagen. The caisson is part of the foundations for a section of the new Oeresund rail-road, bridge-tunnel fixed link across the mouth of the Baltic between east Denmark and south Sweden, due for completion in the year 2000.

--Danish ambassador to Iran Hugo Oestergaard Andersen returned to Denmark at the weekend for consulations with the foreign ministry. All European Union member states bar Greece have taken a series of retaliatory measures against Iran after a German court last week ruled Tehran had ordered the 1992 murders of Kurdish activists in Berlin.

--After years of wage restraint for top executives in the Danish bank sector, major salary increases are now being awarded despite cost cutting campaigns. Top management in Denmark's second and third biggest banks, Unidanmark and BG Bank can expect pay hikes of 20 and 16 percent respectively this year.
--Danish banks' loss and bad debt provisions are set to rise in 1997, a bank expert foresees, regardless of whether or not the economic upturn continues.
